profiles.meeting_scenario: At a tertiary academic cancer center, a planning meeting is being held to prepare the site startup plan for a new phase II precision-oncology platform trial in metastatic colorectal cancer. The trial uses biomarker-directed cohort assignment and depends on molecular prescreening, archival tissue retrieval, and sponsor review before a patient can enter the formal protocol screening window. The protocol synopsis is scientifically attractive, but the center must decide how to operationalize patient identification, specimen flow, and opening readiness over the next six weeks. The agenda is to align on what 'ready to open' means for this study, map the screening workflow around molecular prescreening and the 28-day formal screening clock, decide how existing molecular reports will be used, assign owners for pathology and research tasks, and set the opening timeline. The expected outcome is a shared operational plan with responsibilities, sequencing, and dates for site readiness.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.role: Medical Oncologist and Site Principal Investigator
members.expertise: GI oncology, biomarker-driven trials, investigator-initiated study leadership
members.background: Dr. Park leads the colorectal cancer program at the cancer center and has worked on multiple umbrella and basket studies, mainly from the physician-facing and sponsor-facing side of trial development.
members.private_state: She wants the center seen as an early mover on innovative trial designs and is trying to avoid a slow startup that could shift sponsor attention to competing sites; she also wants the process to feel lightweight enough that treating oncologists will actually refer patients.
hidden_assumptions: If the team says the study is 'ready to open,' that is satisfied once physicians can start discussing the trial with likely candidates and send tissue for sponsor review, even if every downstream site workflow is not yet fully exercised.

When people mention the 'screening workflow,' they mostly mean the front-end path from candidate identification through consent and biomarker matching, with the formal protocol screening window beginning only after a likely match is identified.

Recent molecular profiling in the chart usually means the institution's standard colorectal NGS panel from routine care, which is good enough to identify likely cohort fits unless the protocol clearly says otherwise.

Monitoring whether the screening strategy is 'working' mainly means seeing whether the patients being identified actually yield biomarker matches, rather than whether they clear every operational hurdle on time.

members.name: Maria Alvarez
members.expertise: Trial startup, regulatory coordination, oncology workflow implementation, specimen logistics for precision-medicine studies
members.background: Maria oversees activation and operational readiness for interventional oncology trials across the institution and has extensive experience translating complex protocols into workable processes involving pathology, central labs, research coordinators, and sponsor-required timelines.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid another trial that appears launch-ready from the investigator side but immediately runs into missed windows, specimen problems, and preventable screen failures once patients start moving through the process.
hidden_assumptions: If the team says the study is 'ready to open,' that means the site can begin real patient movement immediately without exposing early candidates to avoidable workflow gaps, including specimen routing, sponsor review, and coordinator handoff.

The screening workflow for this study includes all protocol-relevant steps inside the path to enrollment that can cause a patient to miss the 28-day screening window, especially archival block retrieval, central assay routing, specimen adequacy review, and sponsor turnaround.

When colleagues refer to 'recent molecular profiling,' they usually mean molecular information that is protocol-recognizable for trial triage, ideally the sponsor's designated central assay or a report explicitly acceptable under the eligibility language.

When the team agrees to monitor screen-failure rate to see whether screening is working, the operationally meaningful question is how many consented patients fail to reach enrollment because tissue, timing, or sponsor-review steps break down within the screening path.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the study to be 'ready to open'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss getting the trial 'ready to open' by next month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the site can start physician outreach, patient discussions, and biomarker prescreening activities so that likely candidates can begin moving toward the study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the site can start moving actual candidates through the real study pathway immediately, with research coordination, specimen routing, sponsor review, and screening-window dependencies already functioning reliably.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'ready to open' is informal and common in planning meetings, so it sounds naturally shared; both are aiming for the same calendar milestone and neither has reason to unpack the threshold hidden inside the phrase.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'screening workflow'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to map the 'screening workflow' and keep it as streamlined as possible.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats screening workflow as the front-end process of finding likely candidates, reviewing existing biomarker information, discussing the study, consenting, and identifying who appears matchable before formal protocol screening fully starts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats screening workflow as including the operational chain that must succeed within the protocol screening path, especially pathology block request timing, archival tissue release, central assay shipment, specimen adequacy review, and completing sponsor-required steps inside the 28-day screening window.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are plausible in precision-oncology practice because 'screening' is often used loosely to cover both prescreening and formal screening; the phrase feels routine enough that neither person thinks to draw the boundary explicitly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss using 'recent molecular profiling' already in the chart to avoid unnecessary delays.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the institution's local 468-gene NGS panel performed during routine care within the last few months, which she sees as sufficient for identifying likely cohort fits during prescreening.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of molecular information that the protocol and sponsor would recognize for actual trial triage, ideally the designated central assay package or an explicitly acceptable external report aligned to the biomarker definitions and specimen rules.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about legitimate molecular reports and both are trying to reduce delay, so the phrase sounds concrete enough on its face; neither expects the other to be pointing to a different class of test.

misalignment_points.topic: How to tell whether the screening strategy is 'working'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to monitor the screen-failure rate to ensure the screening strategy is working.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will interpret that mainly as a readout of biological hit-rate: whether the patients being identified through clinic review and existing molecular data are actually yielding biomarker matches.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will interpret it mainly as a readout of process reliability: whether consented patients are being lost because tissue cannot be obtained, specimens are inadequate, central turnaround is too slow, or sponsor review pushes them past the screening window.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Screen-failure rate is a standard phrase that sounds objective and shared, so both assume they are referencing the same familiar metric; the hidden difference is not the label but what each person silently counts as evidence that the strategy is functioning.

turns.inner_thought: I need us aligned on saying this study is ready to open next month. If we can get clinicians comfortable identifying likely candidates, start trial conversations, and begin sending likely fits forward, that is enough to create momentum and keep the sponsor seeing us as engaged. I do not want this bogged down by every downstream operational detail before we can even start.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I'd really like us to have this platform trial ready to open next month. The main goal today is to pin down the startup sequence so we can move quickly but still be sensible about it.

turns.inner_thought: Next month is reasonable only if ready to open means the actual patient path can run on day one without the usual startup holes. I need the plan to cover the real path from identification through the sponsor-facing parts, and when I say screening workflow I mean the whole chain that can make someone miss the 28-day window. I won't unpack that unless I have to.
turns.utterance: That timeline can work from my side. I just want the opening plan to reflect the real patient pathway from the first identification step all the way through the sponsor-facing pieces, and I think if we map the screening workflow carefully now, it will save us trouble later.

turns.inner_thought: The easiest way to keep this light is to start with the patients we already know and the local colorectal NGS results already sitting in the chart. For me, screening workflow is mostly that front-end process of finding likely matches, talking to them early, and not creating a huge burden on clinic before we even know they are plausible candidates.
turns.utterance: I agree. To keep the screening workflow streamlined, I'd start with patients who already have recent molecular profiling in the chart and have physicians begin those conversations early with the likely matches. That should help us avoid unnecessary delays at the front end.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, but I need the team to remember that screening workflow doesn't stop at the front end. It includes the operational steps that can fail once someone is moving toward enrollment, and those are exactly what tend to trip these studies up. I'll keep it general out loud so it still sounds like we're aligned.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. As we do that, I'd like us to map the screening workflow in a way that stays as streamlined as possible once patients start moving through it, especially given the timeline pressures in the protocol.

turns.inner_thought: Most of my refractory colorectal patients already have our routine institutional panel, often from the last few months, so candidate finding should be straightforward. We should not act as if every patient starts from zero. If treating oncologists can quickly see likely cohort fits from what's already in the chart, referrals will actually happen.
turns.utterance: I don't think identifying candidates will be the hard part here. Most of our refractory colorectal patients already have recent molecular profiling, so we should be able to find promising patients without adding much friction for the clinics.

turns.inner_thought: I need to verify what counts as recent molecular profiling for sponsor triage, because local reports may not be enough for what actually moves a patient forward under the protocol. At the same time, pathology support has to be lined up early or we'll lose time immediately. I'll frame this as routine confirmation.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. I'll confirm what pathways we can use for recent molecular profiling and make sure the supporting pieces are lined up on the operations side so we don't create avoidable delays.

turns.inner_thought: Once physician outreach is underway and coordinators know who to review, I would consider us effectively ready to open. I do not want the startup bar set so high that we miss the month and look slow compared with other sites. The details can keep maturing while we begin generating candidates.
turns.utterance: From my perspective, if physician outreach is in place and coordinators know how to start reviewing candidates, we'll effectively be ready to open. I don't want us to lose time waiting for everything to feel completely settled before we start building momentum.

turns.inner_thought: I need the opening date tied to a functioning workflow for real patient movement, not just awareness and prescreening. I'll respond supportively and put named owners around the pieces that matter operationally, but I won't spell out that my threshold for ready to open is much stricter than hers.
turns.utterance: Understood. What I'll do, then, is assign owners across the screening workflow and opening checklist so that the opening date lines up with something people can follow consistently from the start.

turns.inner_thought: Early on, I want a quick signal about whether our clinic review and use of existing molecular data are actually surfacing biologically matchable patients. For me, screen-failure rate is a good readout of whether the screening strategy is working in that sense, and whether our preselection is too broad or appropriately focused.
turns.utterance: One thing I'd like us to watch early is the screen-failure rate, just to make sure the screening strategy is working once we get the first patients moving.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and I will read that as a process metric: are patients falling out because of tissue, timing, handoff, or sponsor-review breakdowns? If the screen-failure rate is high early, I will assume the workflow is not stable enough yet, regardless of how strong the initial candidate identification looks.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The early screen-failure rate should give us a useful read on whether the screening strategy is working and where we may need to tighten things up.

turns.inner_thought: This division of labor lets me focus on physician buy-in and candidate flow while Maria handles the process map. As long as her team owns the screening workflow and opening checklist, I can keep the clinical side light enough that people will actually refer and we can say we're on track for next month.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll take physician engagement and candidate identification, and your team can map the screening workflow and the opening checklist. That should keep us moving on both fronts without overloading the clinics.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send a six-week plan that, in my mind, defines true readiness to open as operational readiness for actual patient flow, clarifies what forms of molecular information are acceptable for real trial use, and tracks process-related screen failures in month one. She'll hear it as support for the launch timeline, which is fine if I can build the guardrails into the document.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll circulate a six-week plan that covers readiness to open, recent molecular profiling pathways, specimen logistics, and a first-month screen-failure tracker so we can see quickly how the startup is performing.
